In a smart lighting prototype 3 implementation effort led by University of Calabria, Italy, the system was able to save around 65% of energy when compared to the traditional system and up to 39% with respect to the LED upgraded system (Gagliardi, 2018). The city of Gothenburg in Sweden has installed ALS for road lighting over a 5-year period (2007–2012) at 20 sites with approximately 1,800 lamps implemented (Al-Haji, 2014). The estimation today is that the average energy consumption per luminaire is reduced to less than 50%. Similarly, Cambridge, Massachusetts, observed a reduction in total energy of about 80% and saved a half-million dollars per year by converting to LEDs and using an adaptive lighting control system (Echelon, 2016). Generally, to recoup the costs of installation required when converting to LEDs takes between 3 and 5 years. Continual advancements in lighting and adaptive control technologies will shorten the payback period, as well as increase the amount of energy savings (Clanton & Associates & VTTI, 2014; Echelon Corporation, 2016). 2.2 Effects of Street Lighting The impact of roadway and street lighting can be considered in terms of both safety and security. Additional impacts on flora and fauna and sky glow are also considerations in an adaptive lighting environment; however, for this project safety and security are the primary analysis factors. 2.2.1 Safety The primary impact of lighting on safety is through the provision of additional visibility. Being able to see pedestrians and objects in the roadway is critical for safe travel. 2.2.1.1 Nighttime Safety It is commonly believed that nighttime driving involves more risks compared to daytime. Keck found that 80% of the vehicle miles driven in 1988 in the United States were in daylight hours but more than half of the fatalities occurred during the night hours (Keck, 1991). In 2007, around 4,620 fatalities and 103,301 traffic related injuries were reported in France. Less than 10% of the traffic but 32% of injuries and 44% of fatalities occurred at night (ONISR, 2006). The accident rates and severity index, in terms of fatal and serious injuries, are almost 2-3 times higher at night than in daylight despite only about 20% of traffic flow taking place at night (Al-Haji, 2014). 2.2.1.2 Pedestrian Safety Pedestrians were found to be at greater risk and more vulnerable than vehicle occupants during nighttime (Wanvik, 2009; Rumar, 1998; Al-Haji, 2008). The U.S. pedestrian accident report investigated data from 1997 to 2006 and found that 66% of the pedestrian fatalities occurred between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. (Chang, 2008). It was also found that pedestrian fatality probability was higher at night (0.20 between 3 a.m. and 6 a.m. vs. below 0.05 during daytime; Figure 1). 4 Figure 1.
